articles.title: Agentic Commerce Is About To Become A Contracting Problem
articles.content:
Much of the conversation about agentic commerce begins with a consumer asking an AI agent to find a flight, order groceries, or buy a pair of shoes.
The technical questions are fascinating. How will the agent verify identity? How will it discover products, compare options, communicate with sellers, and complete payment? Which protocols will allow agents and commercial systems to interact?
But B2B commerce adds a more difficult question: On what terms may the agent transact?
Consumer transactions often occur within standardized structures. The buyer selects a product, accepts the seller’s terms, provides payment, and receives the goods or services. The transaction may involve significant legal complexity, but the consumer agent is usually choosing among options within rules established by the seller.
B2B transactions are different. The terms may be negotiated. Authority may be divided among legal, procurement, finance, security, privacy, and the business. The agreement may create continuing obligations involving data, service levels, insurance, audits, indemnification, renewal, termination, and regulatory compliance.
An agent cannot solve those issues by finding the right product and confirming that a payment method works.
Imagine a procurement agent selecting a software provider. It compares functionality and price, confirms budget availability, and identifies a preferred vendor. The systems can communicate. The agent can authenticate itself. The payment infrastructure is ready.
Then the vendor proposes its standard agreement.
Can the agent accept a limitation of liability based on 12 months of fees? Can it agree to automatic renewal? May the supplier use company data to improve its products? Does the agent have authority to accept a particular governing law, audit restriction, or indemnity obligation?
Technical interoperability does not answer any of those questions. The systems may be perfectly capable of completing the transaction while the agent lacks authority to make the underlying commitments.
This is where agentic commerce becomes a contracting problem.
In B2B settings, the agent must understand more than the agreement in front of it. It needs the company’s preferred positions, acceptable fallbacks, prohibited terms, and approval requirements. It needs to recognize when a commercially attractive deal creates an unacceptable legal or operational risk. It also needs to know who can authorize an exception.
Even after signature, the contract continues to matter. The agent may need to monitor performance, approve invoices, enforce service credits, manage usage rights, provide notices, or decide whether to renew. A B2B transaction is not a single moment of exchange. It is often the beginning of an ongoing governed relationship.
Lawyers should enter the agentic-commerce conversation before these systems are fully designed. If they arrive later, contractual controls may be treated as friction to be added around an already functioning commercial process. That is how companies end up with agents technically capable of acting but poorly governed when they do.
The legal team’s role is not to slow every transaction or require a human lawyer at every step. It is to help distinguish routine decisions that can be delegated from commitments that require judgment or approval.
That means asking practical questions now. Which transactions may an agent complete under standard terms? What monetary, legal, or operational thresholds change its authority? Which provisions always require review? How should conflicts among legal, procurement, finance, and business rules be resolved? How will the company record what the agent agreed to and why?
It also means making contracting logic usable. A folder containing template agreements and a playbook full of phrases such as “commercially reasonable” will not provide enough direction. Agents will need structured positions, contextual rules, and clear escalation paths.
Agentic commerce is often presented as a new channel for buying and selling. In B2B markets, it will also become a new channel for creating legal obligations.
The companies preparing the technical stack should prepare the contractual stack too. Otherwise, their agents may know exactly how to transact without knowing whether they should.
Olga V. Mack is the CEO of TermScout, where she builds legal systems that make contracts faster to understand, easier to operate, and more trustworthy in real business conditions. Her work focuses on how legal rules allocate power, manage risk, and shape decisions under uncertainty. A serial CEO and former General Counsel, Olga previously led a legal technology company through acquisition by LexisNexis. She teaches at Berkeley Law and is a Fellow at CodeX, the Stanford Center for Legal Informatics. She has authored several books on legal innovation and technology, delivered six TEDx talks, and her insights regularly appear in Forbes, Bloomberg Law, VentureBeat, TechCrunch, and Above the Law. Her work treats law as essential infrastructure, designed for how organizations actually operate.

articles.title: Pitchforks To The Barricades!
articles.content:
Unlike most people, I was proud of America in the year 2000, when George Bush and Al Gore played the presidential election to a tie.
I told folks at the time: “In most countries, if an election were a tie, competing mobs would take to the streets. Not in America. We figure that ‘boys will be boys.’ These political morons will work it out somehow. Someone will be sworn in on January 20, and life will go on.”
An event that would have triggered panic elsewhere triggered only yawns in the United States.
Good for us.
I have a “boys will be boys” approach to many political things. For example: Hunter Biden profited on his father’s name? Boys will be boys.
Trump was a little more flagrant than Hunter and extracted billions for himself and his children?
The Democrats pioneered this bullshit. Or at least the Democrats went along with it. Trump was just a little more exuberant about his profiteering.
Biden cancelled a few billion in student debt just before the 2024 elections? Boys will be boys.
Trump sent out Medicare Part B and ObamaCare “refund” checks in anticipation of this year’s election?
The Democrats were the trailblazers. Trump’s gasoline just turned the smoldering trail into a conflagration.
Now, when I hear about the various way that Republicans may try to overturn the results of the midterm elections, I feel the same.
Trump will cause the Postal Service to screw around with mail-in ballots? Boys will be boys.
He’ll send out ICE agents to deter voting by immigrants? Boys will be boys. Federal troops? Eh.
Pressure officials to change election results? Seize voting machines? Have “election monitors” interfere with voting? I assume that lawsuits, or energized voters, or bipartisan objections by all Democrats and all Republican patriots (who aren’t running for reelection) will overcome that.
But there’s one stunt that even I won’t stomach.
The idea is that, before January 3, 2027, House Speaker Mike Johnson replaces the clerk of the House of Representatives with a Trump loyalist. That loyalist clerk, charged with preparing the roll of members-elect for use on January 3, leaves a bunch of Democrats off the roll (because of election irregularities, or whatever).
Without those Democrats on the roll, the listed members-elect — a majority of whom are Republican — elect a Republican Speaker of the House. That Republican Speaker, supported by lickspittle Republican members of the House (or do I repeat myself?), then organize the House and use the power of the majority to refuse to seat the omitted members — preserving a Republican majority for the next two years.
Even for me — a person who’s “boys will be boys” to the core — that would be a bridge too far.
If that happens, join me in grabbing your pitchforks and heading to the barricades.
We’re off to the Bastille.
Mark Herrmann spent 17 years as a partner at a leading international law firm and later oversaw litigation, compliance and employment matters at a large international company. He is the author of The Curmudgeon’s Guide to Practicing Law and Drug and Device Product Liability Litigation Strategy (affiliate links). You can reach him by email at inhouse@abovethelaw.com.
The post Pitchforks To The Barricades! appeared first on Above the Law.

articles.title: Legal Ethics Roundup: Who Gets To Call Themselves A Lawyer?, Judge Pulls Gun In Court, Law Firms That Capitulated, Prosecutorial Misconduct, ABA DQ Bid Rejected, AI + A2J & More
articles.content:
Ed. note: Please welcome Renee Knake Jefferson back to the pages of Above the Law. Subscribe to her Substack, Legal Ethics Roundup, here.
Hello from Boston. Fall leaves are emerging along the Charles River. I’m here this week for a conference. More about that in the “On My Calendar” section below. Let’s dive into the headlines.
#1 “New White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia’s Legal Career Draws Scrutiny.” From Reuters: “Renee Knake Jefferson, a University of Houston law professor and legal ethics expert, said the debate over Zacharia’s status is a ‘fundamental matter of public trust’ that goes beyond ‘professional semantics.’ ‘Of course it goes without saying that one needn’t be a lawyer to serve as the White House press secretary,’ Jefferson said. ‘The public is entitled to accurate information about whether a government official is claiming to hold a professional role that they do not, which is what has been alleged here.’” Read more here. (She didn’t even last the week in the job.)
#2 “Reflections on Lawyering: Accountability for the Law Firms That Capitulated.” From the Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University Blog: “The deals law firms made with the Trump administration are a matter of enormous public interest: They go to the heart of public confidence in the integrity of the legal profession. The public has a right to know what these firms agreed to and what justifications they can offer for their decisions. As part of the Knight Institute’s project on the role of the legal profession in an age of authoritarianism, we recorded a six-episode podcast, Lawyering Without Law. … We interviewed top scholars and former government lawyers on the unique and important role that lawyers play in defending democracy, or in facilitating the slide into authoritarianism. The complete podcast series is available here or wherever you get your podcasts.” Read more here.
#3 “A Bridge or Substitute for Justice.” From The Practice – Harvard Center on the Legal Profession: “On Zoom, Gerald Abila turns his computer screen around, unblurs the background, and asks, ‘Do you see? There’s Winnie.’ Abila sits in Kampala, Uganda, where he runs an NGO, BarefootLaw, trying to reimagine how to deliver legal access to remote populations across his country. … In this article, we think through how the use of AI in the access-to-justice space requires larger systemic thinking around governance, policy, and risk. We speak to Abila about how his initial excitement around AI has worn down; to Themba Mahleka and Nate Edwards, applied researchers in the Pathfinders for Peaceful, Just and Inclusive Societies program at the NYU Center on International Cooperation (CIC), about why AI governance has to be a multistate, multilateral solution; and, finally, to Drew Simshaw, professor of law at the William S. Boyd School of Law at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, about the need for interoperability and a proposal for a national sandbox for innovation.” Read more here.
#4 “Trump Administration Seeks to Remove Judge Who Rebuked It Over Tree Removal.” From The Washington Post: “The Trump administration asked a federal judge Friday to recuse herself from the legal battle over its planned overhaul of East Potomac Golf Links, accusing her of bias and ‘animus’ toward the administration after she sharply rebuked government attorneys over the clearing of hundreds of trees from the public golf course.” Read more here (gift link).
#5 “Court Denies Bid to End Susman ABA Representation in Trump Suit.” From Bloomberg Law: “A federal judge on Friday rejected a Justice Department bid to disqualify Susman Godfrey from representing the American Bar Association in a lawsuit that accuses the Trump administration of carrying out a law firm intimidation policy. Justice Department attorneys had argued that the law firm was a ‘central player’ and a ‘fact witness’ in the litigation, though US District Judge Amir Ali wrote that lawyers for the ABA in the case are ‘not likely to be necessary witnesses.’” Read more here.
#6 “New Mexico Judge Tosses Charges Against Actor Timothy Busfield, Citing Prosecutor Misconduct.” From the Associated Press: “A New Mexico judge has dismissed an indictment against West Wing and Field of Dreams actor Timothy Busfield that accused him of criminal sexual contact with a child, citing prosecutorial misconduct and errors that undermined the grand jury process. State District Judge Joseph Montano granted a defense motion to toss the charges in a decision released Friday. Busfield has repeatedly denied the allegations, describing them as lies motivated by revenge. In an email Friday, Busfield’s attorney Amber Fayerberg said he was ‘relieved and grateful’ after reading the judge’s decision.” Read more here.
#7 “Gun-Toting NYC Judge Censured by Ethics Board for Bizarre ‘Little Experiment’ in Court.” From the New York Post: “A gun-toting New York City judge who pulled out a pistol in court to ‘deceive’ a testifying police officer was admonished by a state judicial ethics commission for his ‘little experiment,’ according to an announcement Tuesday. Criminal court Judge Jeffrey Gershuny whipped out his personal gun to challenge whether a testifying police officer back in 2025 could have actually identified if a suspect was carrying the weapon in a shopping bag. But as he went to pull out his personal 9mm pistol — to the discomfort of court officers in the room — he actually hid the gun on the ground and placed a stapler in a shopping bag in a bid to trick the cop. It was a bizarre move that the New York State Commission on Judicial Conduct said deserves official censure.” Read more here.
#8 “US Judge Facing Misconduct Claims Said to Have ‘Abandoned’ Job.” From Bloomberg Law: “A committee of judicial investigators said that a federal judge in Dallas abandoned her role and recommended she be temporarily stripped of her docket, according to internal court documents shared with Bloomberg Law.” Read more here.
#9 “Rethinking the Legal Profession’s Role in Business and Human Rights.” From the Center for Strategic and International Studies: “Short of structural changes, there are also several concrete demands that civil society has made and legislation could address: access to remedy, a due diligence requirement for U.S. supply chains, and the use of litigation to silence critics. Lawyers matter in each of these areas in two respects. As advisers, they shape the scope of corporate due diligence, determine what is documented, and influence whether troubling findings prompt action and, if so, what action. As advocates, they decide how to respond to those who raise concerns. The American Bar Association’s Resolution 604, adopted in August 2024, addresses both roles: It urges lawyers to counsel clients on human rights and environmental due diligence beyond minimum legal requirements and to abstain from abuse of process.” Read more here.
#10 “Atty Sanctioned For Vulgar Emails To Opposing Counsel.” From Law360: “A Texas federal magistrate judge has sanctioned an attorney who serves as principal for an oil and gas exploration company locked in a trade secret misappropriation case with a rival after opposing counsel complained of his expletive-ridden emails containing ad hominem attacks.” Read more here.
For the first half of the week, I’m participating in the Women Execs on Boards Global Symposium at the David Rubenstein Treehouse at Harvard University. But then it’s back to Texas, and a special weekend to celebrate my birthday by attending the Formula 1 Grand Prix in Austin with my husband and kids. The kids started following the races nearly a decade ago when we lived within earshot of the Australian Grand Prix during my stint as the Fulbright Distinguished Chair of Entrepreneurship and Innovation at Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology University. I probably won’t be getting behind the wheel of a race car this time, but you never know!
Looking for other upcoming ethics events? You’ll find a list here.
Renee Knake Jefferson holds the endowed Doherty Chair in Legal Ethics and is a Professor of Law at the University of Houston. Check out more of her writing at the Legal Ethics Roundup. Find her on X (formerly Twitter) at @reneeknake or Bluesky at legalethics.bsky.social.
The post Legal Ethics Roundup: Who Gets To Call Themselves A Lawyer?, Judge Pulls Gun In Court, Law Firms That Capitulated, Prosecutorial Misconduct, ABA DQ Bid Rejected, AI + A2J & More appeared first on Above the Law.
